analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines hantaviruses (family Hantaviridae) and their pandemic potential, focusing on the Andes virus (ANDV) as the only hantavirus with documented human-to-human transmission, while contrasting hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Europe/Asia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in the Americas with high mortality. The central question is whether hantaviruses can cause the next pandemic, particularly in light of the 2026 MV Hondius ANDV outbreak.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is narrative in type and synthesizes current knowledge on hantaviruses, including their zoonotic transmission via rodent-derived aerosols, clinical syndromes, and the 2026 MV Hondius outbreak timeline (April 1–May 13, 2026) with 11 confirmed ANDV cases and 3 deaths (27% case fatality rate). The supplied evidence does not report databases, search dates, eligibility criteria, selection methods, or included-study counts.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: ANDV is the only hantavirus with confirmed human-to-human transmission, demonstrated during the 2026 MV Hondius outbreak, which resulted in 11 confirmed cases and 3 deaths (27% case fatality rate). Hantaviruses share pandemic-associated features such as zoonotic origin, RNA genome variability, and environmental influences, but most hantaviruses lack human-to-human transmissibility.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights uncertainty regarding the pandemic potential of hantaviruses beyond ANDV, given the absence of documented human-to-human transmission for other hantaviruses despite shared genomic and ecological features. The 2026 MV Hondius outbreak’s limited scale and confined setting (cruise ship) leave unresolved questions about broader transmission dynamics in non-close-contact settings.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Priority research should focus on characterizing transmission mechanisms of ANDV and other hantaviruses in diverse settings, including non-close-contact environments, to assess pandemic risk. Surveillance systems should integrate hantavirus diagnostics and genomic sequencing to detect emerging variants and transmission chains, particularly in regions with rodent reservoirs.

analysis.summary_en: This review evaluates whether hantaviruses can cause pandemics, centering on Andes virus (ANDV) as the sole hantavirus with proven human-to-human transmission, exemplified by the 2026 MV Hondius outbreak (11 cases, 3 deaths; 27% case fatality rate). It contrasts hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Europe/Asia with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in the Americas, noting high mortality in HCPS. While hantaviruses share pandemic-associated features like zoonotic origin and RNA variability, most lack human-to-human transmissibility. Key gaps include unresolved transmission dynamics beyond close-contact scenarios and limited evidence on broader pandemic potential. Research priorities include transmission mechanism studies, enhanced surveillance with genomic sequencing, and diagnostic integration to detect emerging variants and chains of transmission.

title: Spatiotemporal correlation analysis between climate change and hantavirus outbreak in Argentina: Quantitative causal inference based on Google Earth Engine and Bayesian spatiotemporal regression

analysis.research_question_and_background: Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS) cases in Argentina rose sharply to 101 in 2025–2026, with a geographic shift from Patagonia to Buenos Aires and the northwest NOA region. The study addresses whether climate anomalies such as high temperature, drought, and heavy rainfall are spatiotemporally correlated with and causally linked to hantavirus outbreaks.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used national HPS case data from 2020 to 2026 from Argentina’s Ministry of Health, WHO, and PAHO, extracting onset dates and geographic coordinates. Climate data were integrated via Google Earth Engine using ERA5-Land and NOAA GSOD datasets at 0.1° resolution.
analysis.methods: Monthly climate anomalies (temperature, precipitation via SPI, soil moisture) and extreme weather frequencies were calculated in GEE. Bayesian Spatiotemporal Poisson Regression with INLA estimated lagged effects (1–6 months) and spatial heterogeneity. Causal Mediation Analysis identified the pathway from climate anomalies to vegetation productivity, rodent expansion, and human exposure.
analysis.main_results: HPS cases in 2025–2026 showed unstable spatial distribution (Moran’s I = 0.42, p < 1.5). Outbreaks in NOA were associated with drought-flood compound events after persistent drought. Vegetation index (NDVI) mediated 41.2% of climate–HPS risk in Buenos Aires and 56.7% in NOA.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study confirms a causal pathway where drought-flood compound events drive rodent population expansion and human exposure via vegetation changes, representing the first national-scale quantitative causal inference of climate–hantavirus dynamics in Argentina.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings support the development of a GEE-based real-time monitoring framework for an HPS Climate-Driven Early Warning System in Argentina, enabling targeted surveillance and prevention in high-risk regions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on ecological associations and modeled mediation, which may not capture all confounders or individual-level exposures, limiting causal inference strength despite advanced spatiotemporal modeling.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the spatiotemporal correlation and causal pathways between climate anomalies and hantavirus outbreaks in Argentina during 2020–2026. Using national HPS case data and high-resolution climate datasets processed in Google Earth Engine, the authors applied Bayesian spatiotemporal Poisson regression and causal mediation analysis to quantify lagged effects and mediating vegetation dynamics. The 2025–2026 HPS season saw 101 cases with a shift from Patagonia to Buenos Aires and the NOA region, where drought-flood compound events were closely linked to outbreaks. Vegetation productivity mediated 41.2% to 56.7% of the climate–HPS risk across regions. The authors conclude that drought-flood events drive rodent expansion and human exposure via trophic cascades, proposing a GEE-based early warning system for HPS risk in Argentina.

analysis.summary_en: There are two major clinical syndromes associated with human infections: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) — mostly reported from Europe and Asia, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) — mostly reported from the Americas. The Middle East has a relatively low incidence of hantavirus disease, but recent epidemiological studies have shown that the virus is circulating in several countries, including Türkiye and Iran. Current data suggest that while human infections are rare, ecological conditions which could sustain hantavirus are present in several Middle Eastern countries, and therefore increased surveillance and research into interdisciplinary and One Health initiatives are needed. Creating closer ties between the medical, veterinary and environmental communities is crucial for early outbreak detection and prevention in the future.

title: Modeling the Transmission Dynamics of Hantavirus with Environmental Viral Persistence

analysis.research_question_and_background: Hantavirus is a zoonotic infection maintained principally in rodent reservoirs, and human exposure occurs mainly through environments contaminated with infectious viral particles.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study formulates and analyses a deterministic compartmental model for hantavirus transmission involving susceptible and infected rodents, susceptible, exposed, infectious and recovered humans, and an environmental viral reservoir.
analysis.methods: The model includes logistic rodent growth, direct rodent-to-rodent transmission, indirect environmental transmission, viral shedding from infected classes and natural viral clearance.

analysis.summary_en: Hantavirus is a zoonotic infection maintained principally in rodent reservoirs, and human exposure occurs mainly through environments contaminated with infectious viral particles. This study formulates and analyses a deterministic compartmental model for hantavirus transmission involving susceptible and infected rodents, susceptible, exposed, infectious and recovered humans, and an environmental viral reservoir. The model includes logistic rodent growth, direct rodent-to-rodent transmission, indirect environmental transmission, viral shedding from infected classes and natural viral clearance. Stability analysis shows that the disease-free equilibrium is locally and globally asymptotically stable when R0 1 and the existence of a biologically feasible endemic equilibrium. These findings suggest that reducing rodent infection, limiting environmental contamination and increasing viral clearance may help move the system below the epidemic threshold. The analysis indicates that environmental viral persistence provides an indirect pathway that can sustain transmission between infected rodents, susceptible rodents and humans. The model offers a mathematically tractable framework for interpreting hantavirus persistence and for guiding future extensions involving seasonality, spatial structure, stochasticity and data-driven parameterisation.

Therefore, this study aimed to determine the long-term storage conditions for the developed multiplex ICA strips. Therefore, we have previously developed a multiplex immunochromatographic assay (ICA) to detect antibodies against six pathogens as follows: mouse hepatitis virus, Sendai virus, and Clostridium piliforme (Tyzzer's disease) in mice, and Seoul type orthohantavirus, Sendai virus, and sialodacryoadenitis virus in rats. However, when stored at 18-28 °C (room temperature) and 4 °C, the detectable reactivity of the multiplex ICA strips stored in poly_bags was reduced for some of the six targets pathogens at 18 months after storage. The oxygen absorber reduced detectability of the multiplex ICA strips. Serological monitoring of infectious diseases in laboratory rodents is vital for ensuring animal health. These results indicate that storing ICA strips in poly_bags at -30 °C, which is a simple method, is able to maintain detectability long-term for the strips format and pathogen targets examined in this study.

In this study, a mathematical modeling framework—including compartmental, small-world (SW), and scale-free (SF) network models—was developed to analyze the dynamics of hantavirus and norovirus transmission on recent cruise ship outbreaks. The results show that when the initial number of exposed or infected individuals is extremely small (e.g., 1–2 persons), disease spread is dominated by stochasticity, causing substantial variation between individual simulations and mean model predictions. The compartmental model, while consistent with average simulation outcomes, failed to reliably predict any single outbreak event.
